claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native oxide film formed under ambient conditions.
The native oxide film on as-received Q235 steel is irregular.
Annealing temperature and duration can control microstructural evolution relevant to corrosion behavior.
Controlled annealing of Q235 steel promotes beneficial phase transformations and densification in its native oxide layer.
An optimum annealing condition produces a more continuous, uniform, and less porous passive film on Q235 steel.
A dense and continuous passive oxide film improves corrosion resistance.
The annealing-induced passive film slows corrosion by impeding chloride penetration.
Insufficient or excessive annealing produces cracks, nonuniform phases, or other defects in the Q235 oxide film.
Defects in the oxide film provide preferential sites for pitting and corrosion degradation, especially during high-temperature salt exposure.
Optimally annealed Q235 steel will show reduced mass change relative to untreated Q235 steel after chloride-salt exposure.
Optimally annealed Q235 steel will show lower pitting density and better film integrity than untreated Q235 steel.
The protection produced by optimum annealing will occur both at room temperature and at 700–900 °C.
Suboptimal annealing treatments will provide little or no corrosion-protection improvement.
Untreated Q235 steel has moderate resistance to salt-induced corrosion.
The proposed mechanism applies predominantly to as-received Q235 steel under aggressive chloride-salt conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in inert or non-corrosive environments or when additional protective coatings are present.
